title: Brandade de Morue
subtitle: Salt cod whipped with olive oil, cream, and garlic
excerpt: Soaked salt cod beaten with warm olive oil, cream, and garlic until it becomes a creamy, spreadable purée. A dish from the Languedoc coast, traditionally served warm with bread or croutons.
sourceNotes: Brandade de morue is the great salt-cod dish of Nîmes and the Languedoc. It appears in Prosper Montagné, Larousse Gastronomique (1938). Elizabeth David, A Book of Mediterranean Food (1950), gives the recipe and notes that the dish was carried to the entire Mediterranean coast by Languedoc traders. The word brandade derives from the Occitan brandar, 'to stir'. The classic Nîmes version contains no potato; the version with potato is Parisian.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Brandade reheats very well. Cover the surface with a thin layer of olive oil to prevent a skin forming. Reheat gently in a low oven (140°C) or in a bowl set over hot water, stirring frequently.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cod preserved by heavy salting and drying. It must be soaked in cold water for 24 to 48 hours before use, changing the water several times, to rehydrate the fish and remove most of the salt. After soaking, salt cod has a firm, flaky texture unlike fresh fish. It is found in the chilled or dried fish section of fishmongers and larger supermarkets.

content.text: Brandade de morue is made from

that has been soaked for 24 hours to remove most of the salt, poached briefly until it flakes, then beaten with warm olive oil and cream until it becomes a smooth, pale, spreadable purée. The texture should be silky enough to coat a piece of toast without being thick. The flavour is intensely savoury with a mild background of garlic.
Begin the day before: the salt cod must soak in cold water for at least 24 hours with several water changes.

items.prepNote: soaked in cold water for 24 hours, changing the water 3 to 4 times
best quality, warmed to body temperature
sliced and toasted or fried in olive oil

content.text: Place the soaked, drained salt cod in a saucepan with the garlic, bay, and thyme. Cover with cold water. Bring to a bare simmer and poach very gently for 10 to 12 minutes until the fish flakes. Drain, reserving 50 ml of the cooking water. Discard the bay and thyme. Keep the poached garlic.
Remove any skin and bones from the fish. Transfer the fish and the poached garlic to the food processor.

With the processor running, slowly pour in the warm olive oil, then the warm cream, alternating between them in small additions, as you would when making mayonnaise. The mixture will come together into a thick, creamy purée.

If the brandade is too thick, thin with a little of the reserved poaching water. If it is too thin, process for a little longer. Taste for seasoning, it will likely need pepper and possibly a little salt, but salt cod is already salty.
Serve warm in a shallow bowl or baking dish, drizzled with olive oil, with croutons alongside.

items.cause: The cod was not soaked long enough, or not enough water changes were made.
items.fix: Salt cod requires a minimum of 24 hours soaking, ideally 36 to 48 hours, with 3 to 4 water changes. Taste the fish after poaching: if it is still very salty, soak for longer next time. Increase the cream slightly to balance the salt in the existing batch.

items.symptom: The texture is grainy rather than smooth
items.cause: The cod fibres were not properly broken down, or the oil and cream were added too quickly.
items.fix: Process for longer, and add the liquid more slowly. The oil and cream must be warm, cold liquid causes the mixture to seize. If it has seized, try adding a little more warm cream and processing again.

items.cause: The oil or cream was too cold, or added too fast.
items.fix: Remove from the processor and whisk vigorously with a little warm water. Like a broken mayonnaise, it can be rescued by slowly incorporating a small amount of warm liquid.

content.text: Brandade de morue is the principal dish of Nîmes, the Roman city in the Languedoc. Salt cod reached the Mediterranean coast from the northern European fishing trade in the Middle Ages. It quickly became a staple ingredient in southern France, Spain, Portugal, and Italy. The Nîmes version uses only cod, olive oil, and garlic, without potato. The Provençal version and most modern adaptations include potato, which lightens the texture and stretches the expensive fish further. The dish is closely associated with the Lenten calendar, when no meat was eaten, and is still served on Good Friday across southern France.
